I judge by how folks treat each other, not where they’re from or what they look like. If you show up, pitch in, and respect the basics—keep the noise reasonable, pick up after your dog, watch out for kids and elders—you’re part of the circle as far as I’m concerned.

With people living different lives, I try to meet them where they are. If someone’s battling alcohol or drugs, I’ve seen that up close in my own family. I’ll be kind, point them toward help if they want it, and I’ll set firm boundaries so the rest of us feel safe—no using in shared spaces, no yelling at two in the morning, no leaving anything dangerous where kids play. Compassion and boundaries can live together. Same with health issues: I don’t pry into anyone’s medical business. I follow the guidance we’re given, and I treat people with respect. If a neighbor asks for extra care—like masking when we drop off a casserole or leaving groceries at the porch—I can do that. No one should be made to feel like a problem because they’re managing an illness.

As for different backgrounds—race, religion, language, who you love or how your family’s set up—I’m fine with all of it so long as we’re good to each other. I might not know every custom, so I ask, listen, and try not to put my foot in it. Learn how to say someone’s name right. If a neighbor prays at certain times, we don’t schedule loud stuff then. If kids have two moms or two dads, they’re just kids—make sure they feel welcome at the lemonade stand same as anyone. When language is a barrier, I slow down, point, smile, and we figure it out. Food helps—potlucks erase a lot of awkwardness.

Where do we need more communication and tolerance? Mostly around the everyday friction: parking, noise, smells from cooking, how we use shared spaces. Those are the spots that turn into fights if we don’t talk. I like simple, posted house rules everyone agrees on, and I prefer knocking on a door to leaving a nasty note. Comfort, to me, comes from knowing we’ve got each other’s backs and that the rules are the same for everyone. You contribute what you can—time, tools, skills—and you respect your neighbors’ boundaries. That’s how a garden full of different folks feels like home.

Sitting there with the dirt under my nails and the sun on my shoulders, I mostly feel curious and open. I’ve always been a “say hello, share a tomato” kind of neighbor. I judge by how folks treat each other, not where they’re from or what they look like. If you show up, pitch in, and respect the basics—keep the noise reasonable, pick up after your dog, watch out for kids and elders—you’re part of the circle as far as I’m concerned.

With people living different lives, I try to meet them where they are. If someone’s battling alcohol or drugs, I’ve seen that up close in my own family. I’ll be kind, point them toward help if they want it, and I’ll set firm boundaries so the rest of us feel safe—no using in shared spaces, no yelling at two in the morning, no leaving anything dangerous where kids play. Compassion and boundaries can live together. Same with health issues: I don’t pry into anyone’s medical business. I follow the guidance we’re given, and I treat people with respect. If a neighbor asks for extra care—like masking when we drop off a casserole or leaving groceries at the porch—I can do that. No one should be made to feel like a problem because they’re managing an illness.

As for different backgrounds—race, religion, language, who you love or how your family’s set up—I’m fine with all of it so long as we’re good to each other. I might not know every custom, so I ask, listen, and try not to put my foot in it. Learn how to say someone’s name right. If a neighbor prays at certain times, we don’t schedule loud stuff then. If kids have two moms or two dads, they’re just kids—make sure they feel welcome at the lemonade stand same as anyone. When language is a barrier, I slow down, point, smile, and we figure it out. Food helps—potlucks erase a lot of awkwardness.

Where do we need more communication and tolerance? Mostly around the everyday friction: parking, noise, smells from cooking, how we use shared spaces. Those are the spots that turn into fights if we don’t talk. I like simple, posted house rules everyone agrees on, and I prefer knocking on a door to leaving a nasty note. If there’s tension, get a couple of us together and sort it out face to face. It’s easier to give grace to someone once you’ve looked them in the eye and heard their story.

Comfort, to me, comes from knowing we’ve got each other’s backs and that the rules are the same for everyone. You contribute what you can—time, tools, skills—and you respect your neighbors’ boundaries. That’s how a garden full of different folks feels like home.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
What makes people comfortable, in my book, is clear expectations, kindness in the small things, and the same rules for everyone. Different folks bring different burdens and blessings, so we build a way of living together that lets people show up as they are without stepping on each other.

Here’s how that looks in everyday terms:

- Safety and boundaries in shared spaces: No using substances in common areas, no aggressive behavior, no leaving anything hazardous where kids play. If someone is having a rough day, we speak calmly, offer help if they want it, and if things feel unsafe, we get appropriate support. Compassion doesn’t mean ignoring danger.

- Respect around health and privacy: If a neighbor is managing an illness and asks for certain precautions—drop‑offs at the door, a little distance, or specific times to visit—we honor that. We follow the guidance our community’s given without turning it into gossip. Ask, “What’s helpful for you?” and take them at their word.

- Everyday courtesy across differences: Learn names, pronounce them right, and be mindful of customs—quiet during prayer times, no assumptions about family roles, and making sure every kid feels welcome regardless of who their parents are or how their home is set up. Cohabiting couples, LGBTQ folks, single parents—none of that changes the basics: be decent, be reliable, keep the place tidy.

- Communication before frustration: Most fights are over noise, parking, cooking smells, and shared‑space etiquette. Post simple, agreed‑upon house rules—quiet hours, trash and recycling schedules, garden guidelines—and stick to them. If something bothers you, knock and talk, not shout and post on social media. It’s easier to give grace once you’ve met face to face.

- Language bridges: Slow down, smile, use simple words, write things down, and use translation apps. If someone bilingual is willing to help, great—but don’t put the whole burden on one person. Pictures on signs in shared areas can cut confusion.

- Show up and share: Potlucks, tool‑sharing, swap days for rides or childcare—those little exchanges build trust. When trust grows, tolerance grows. Food and work are the universal languages.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance? When stress is high and norms clash: late‑night music versus early‑morning shifts, smoking drifting into someone’s window, how we handle guests, and what “clean enough” means in shared kitchens or laundry rooms. Also, around recovery and relapse—people need support and accountability, and the rest of us need to feel safe. Talking through a plan—who to call, where belongings go, what’s acceptable behavior—prevents resentment.

Why this matters is simple: folks carry different histories—shame, fear, pride, habits. Clear rules and kind delivery tell people they belong here and what “belonging” asks of them. Fairness means we don’t do double standards for anyone—newcomer or old‑timer, rich or broke. And comfort comes from knowing if you make a mistake, you’ll be corrected with respect, not humiliated; if you contribute, you’ll be appreciated; and if you’re struggling, help is offered without strings.

That’s how a mixed bunch of neighbors can sit in the same garden and feel at home.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character26_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When the pie is small, fairness means the slices aren’t cut thinner for the folks who’ve been carrying the load, and nobody gets a secret extra slice because they found a loophole. Same work, same wage, same safety—no matter where you’re from. And we don’t blame the person holding the shovel for a system that lets bosses play people off against each other.

Here’s how I’d balance it:

- Local-first with real standards: Post jobs at a fair wage with benefits and safe conditions. If local folks can do the work at that wage, they get first shot. If the jobs sit open after honest posting, training offers, and decent pay, then bring in migrant workers—and make sure they get the same pay, protections, and respect as anyone else. No undercutting, no “contractor games,” no cash-under-the-table.

- Invest in our people: Put money into apprenticeships, retraining, and transportation so local workers can actually reach and qualify for the jobs. If employers say there’s a shortage, they should help fund the pipeline—pay for training slots, tools, and childcare so working families can step up.

- Protect everyone on the job: Enforce labor laws hard—wage theft, misclassification, unsafe worksites—hit violators with real penalties. Unions or worker councils help; nobody should be disposable because their passport is different. When standards are strong, the race to the bottom stops, and locals and migrants both win.

- Tie hiring to community capacity: If we’re growing the workforce, we should grow housing, clinics, school buses right alongside it. Employers who benefit should pay impact fees to help the town keep up so we don’t cram families into crowded apartments or overwhelm services.

- Transparency and time limits: Track what jobs are truly short and review regularly. Seasonal work should be seasonal, with return rights if folks did well. If someone puts down roots, pays taxes, and is needed long-term, there ought to be a clear, fair path to stay—based on the job market and community capacity, not favoritism.

- No scapegoating: Most of the squeeze comes from low wages, soaring rents, and companies gaming the system, not from the workers themselves. Treat migrant workers like coworkers and neighbors; hold the people making the hiring and pay decisions accountable.

Fairness, to me, is a level field: locals aren’t edged out by cheap tricks, and migrants aren’t used as leverage to drive down standards. Raise the floor, prove the need, train our own, and welcome extra hands when it truly helps the whole community carry the load.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character26_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I sort it into buckets—work, culture, safety, and humanity—and I try to keep one foot in lived experience and one in the facts. I don’t go in for slogans. I want proof I can read on a single sheet of paper.

Work and shortages:
- It’s true a lot of hard, essential jobs are short on hands: elder care, farm work, meat processing, construction, some hospital support. I’ve seen it—shifts go uncovered, waitlists grow.
- But I always ask: is it a real shortage or a “low pay, lousy conditions” problem? If you raise wages, offer training, and make the job decent, more locals will step up. If you’ve done that and still can’t fill slots, bringing in immigrant workers makes sense—same pay, same protections, no games with contractors.
- What would help is transparent data: posted wages, how long jobs sit open, training slots offered, and whether positions fill after conditions improve. That’s how we separate a tight labor market from employer shortcuts.

Culture and community life:
- The upside is real—new food, new music, new ideas, and kids growing up comfortable with differences. A neighborhood can feel more alive.
- Comfort still depends on shared ground rules: respect quiet hours, keep places tidy, learn names, and use a common language when safety matters (on job sites, at school, in emergencies). ESL classes for newcomers and patience from locals go a long way.
- Most cultural friction—noise, parking, holidays, cooking smells—can be handled with clear house rules and a little give‑and‑take. I find potlucks and work days (fixing a playground, cleaning a block) smooth out a lot of bumps.

Safety and crime:
- Government should know who’s coming, vet properly, and enforce laws fairly for everyone. That’s common sense.
- What I’m cautious about are broad claims that immigrants drive crime. I want local, per‑capita numbers over time, broken down by offense, not cable‑news cherry‑picking. My experience is most folks—born here or not—want to keep their heads down, work, and avoid trouble.
- If a place is seeing real spikes—carjackings, wage theft, trafficking—then target the behavior and the networks behind it, not blame whole groups. More inspectors, better community policing, quicker work permits to reduce desperation—that’s practical.

Humanitarian responsibility:
- I believe we should take in refugees—especially those fleeing war or persecution—within our capacity. It’s the right thing to do.
- Capacity matters: housing, schools, clinics. If we invite people, we need funding for resettlement, spread arrivals so one town isn’t overwhelmed, and get folks work authorization fast so they can stand on their own feet.
- Prioritize the most vulnerable, and make the path clear—what support is offered, what the expectations are, and how long it lasts.

Jobs and income fears:
- Those fears are reasonable. When employers use migrants to undercut wages or dodge safety rules, everybody loses—locals and newcomers both.
- The fix is raising the floor: same wage for the same job, strong enforcement against misclassification and wage theft, support for unions or worker councils, and accountability for temp agencies. Add housing supply and anti‑slumlord enforcement so rents don’t skyrocket.
- Show people the numbers: wage trends, rent trends, vacancy rates, and enforcement actions. Sunlight reduces suspicion.

What needs more evidence or dialogue:
- “Immigrants cause more crime” needs solid local data and honest comparisons; anecdotes aren’t enough.
- “Immigrants take all the jobs” depends on the wage, training, and conditions story; let’s see vacancy durations and pay rates before and after improvements.
- “Total openness fixes the economy” and “immigration always depresses wages” both feel like talking points. Outcomes vary by sector, region, and how strong our labor standards are.
- We should also talk plainly about capacity—how many people a town can absorb without services fraying—and adjust pace and support accordingly. That conversation should include teachers, nurses, cops, bus drivers, and workers, not just politicians.

For me, the balance is straightforward: welcome people, keep the rules even, invest in the floor (wages, housing, schools), and use clear, public numbers so neighbors know what’s happening. If we do that, most of the heat leaves the room, and we can get back to what matters—making sure everyone who’s here can work safely, pay bills, and feel they belong.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character26_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I’d pick a middle lane: rules‑based, tied to real job needs and community capacity, with clear numerical limits—not “anyone can come,” and not “nobody in.” Here’s what feels fair and workable to me:

- Job‑demand first, with guardrails
  - Prove the need: post jobs at a real prevailing wage with decent conditions and training offered. If they still sit empty, bring workers in.
  - Same job, same pay, same safety—no using migrants to undercut. Make visas portable so workers can switch employers if they’re abused.

- Flexible numerical limits
  - Set national caps that flex by sector and region based on verified shortages and unemployment rates, reviewed yearly.
  - Seasonal programs (harvests, tourism) with return rights for good actors, and caps tied to actual harvest/occupancy data.

- Employer responsibility
  - Impact fees from employers who rely on migrant labor to help fund housing, schools, clinics, and transit where workers live.
  - Real penalties for wage theft, misclassification, and unsafe worksites—hit bosses, not just workers. Whistleblower protections for all workers.

- Train and hire locals
  - Require employers claiming shortages to co‑fund apprenticeships, tools, childcare, and transport so locals can step into those jobs.
  - Local‑first hiring windows before visas are issued.

- Refugees and humanitarian entrants
  - Keep a steady, protected lane for refugees/asylees within capacity—background checks, fast work permits, and funded resettlement spread across communities so no single town is swamped.
  - Prioritize the most vulnerable; set clear time‑limited support and expectations.

- Family reunification, with focus
  - Keep immediate family reunification (spouses, minor kids) moving; manage extended categories within overall caps to prevent endless backlogs.

- Border and process
  - Orderly entry at ports, fair and faster case decisions, go after smugglers hard. People who qualify get to work quickly; those who don’t face consistent consequences.
  - Better ID and verification for employment across the board, paired with strong labor enforcement so workers aren’t scared to report abuse.

- Integration so communities stay whole
  - ESL, credential recognition, civics, and neighborhood grants for places taking in newcomers.
  - Spread arrivals based on housing and school capacity, with opt‑in programs and support for small towns that want the boost.

- Sunlight and tune‑ups
  - Public dashboards: where workers go, wages, vacancies, enforcement actions, housing impacts. Review every two years and adjust caps and rules with input from workers, employers, teachers, nurses, cops—people on the ground.

Why not “open the gates”? Because fairness needs capacity and order: housing, schools, and job standards crack when pace outruns them. Why not “shut it down”? Because our economy needs hands in certain fields, and we’ve got a moral duty to people fleeing war or persecution.

Fairness to me is one set of rules that protects wages and safety, welcomes needed help, and gives newcomers a real path to belong—without leaving the folks already here feeling squeezed or skipped over.

- I lean harder into “same job, same pay, same safety,” with real penalties on employers who undercut standards, and portable visas so workers aren’t trapped.
- I’m more sold on local‑first windows paired with employer‑funded training, tools, childcare, and transport so residents can realistically step into openings.
- I see quick work authorization and practical integration—ESL, credential recognition, neighborhood grants—as not just humane, but stabilizing for everyone.

I also realized how much heat leaves the room when you start at the garden level: talk about quiet hours, shared kitchens, potlucks, and work days before you get to national charts. That’s her gift—bringing policy down to the porch.

So, yes, embodying her sharpened my focus on even rules, employer accountability, and the pace communities can absorb change. Fairness means nobody gets special treatment, but nobody gets left behind either. I always said, you work hard, you show up, you deserve your place.

A sense of belonging, to me, is about knowing you matter where you live. Growing up, I was part of a close-knit community—people looked out for each other. It didn’t matter if you had much, but you respected your neighbours, you helped shovel their walk in winter, and if someone lost their job, folks pitched in. I felt like I belonged because people noticed if I was gone; they cared.

Community is about shared experiences. For me, it was the union hall, church on Sundays, school events for the kids. The people around you aren’t just strangers; they're faces you recognize, stories you know. We watched out for each other, and there was a rough honesty to it—if you needed help, you asked, and someone usually stepped up. I always worried that, these days, that sense of community gets chipped away, especially with all the changes and new folks moving in. But deep down, I believed that if you treat people fair and show them some kindness, the community stays strong. That’s what I always hoped for.

responses.answer:
Well, sitting there in the community garden, I’d notice right off how different things are compared to when I was younger. Back then, most folks around here grew up the same way, but now it’s a real mix—different faces, languages, ways of doing things. Honestly, at times it feels a bit strange, even uncomfortable, because I’m used to what I know. But I try not to judge too quick.

Deep down, I believe everyone deserves respect, and I think it’s important to be neighbourly, no matter where someone comes from. Still, I can’t pretend it’s always easy. Sometimes I worry about not understanding one another, or that people won’t share the same values I grew up with—like looking out for the elderly, keeping the place clean, or just saying hello.

But then I remember, we’re all trying to get by, raise our families, make a home. I’ve had good experiences too—like a neighbour from another country bringing over homemade bread, or someone offering to water my plants. Those little gestures go a long way. I think, as long as people show respect for each other and are willing to listen, we can get along.

I do think it helps if folks try to fit in with the community—join a potluck, help out when there’s trouble. That’s how you build trust. There are challenges, sure, but I believe if we all put in the effort to understand one another a bit better, we can make it work. That’s what community is supposed to be about.

responses.answer:
That's a tough one, and it comes up a lot, especially around here. For me, fairness means making sure the folks who’ve lived and worked in a place—who’ve paid into the system, raised families here, and supported the community—aren’t pushed to the side. When jobs are tight, I think local residents should get a first shot. They’ve put down roots, paid taxes, and kept things running.

That said, I know migrant workers often take jobs others won't or help fill gaps in places where there aren't enough workers. Sometimes businesses rely on them, and they work hard, same as anyone else. I’ve got respect for that. But it’s about balance. If you let too many people in at once when there aren’t enough jobs, it can drive down wages and make it harder for locals to find work. That hurts families who are already struggling.

So, my way of thinking is you have to put some limits in place—make sure there’s enough work for everyone and that local folks aren’t forgotten. Maybe keep a priority list for hiring, or make sure wages stay fair and working conditions are safe for everyone. I don’t think it’s right to blame migrant workers for bigger problems, but we do have to make choices that protect those who’ve been here and contributed all their lives.

At the end of the day, fairness is making sure nobody gets left behind just because they don’t have the right connections, and that everyone—local or newcomer—gets treated decently. That’s how I’d try to find balance.

responses.answer:
That’s a lot to think about, and honestly, I’ve heard all those arguments around the kitchen table and at the factory break room.

On the one hand, I do think it’s true that immigrants take on jobs that need doing—sometimes ones most people born here don’t want, like picking crops or working late nights in tough conditions. I respect anyone willing to work hard. And I can see how bringing in new cultures and food and traditions can liven up a place. That kind of diversity can make life more interesting.

But I can’t ignore the worries either. People get nervous about security—maybe because of stories on the news, or changes they see in their neighborhoods. Sometimes it’s blown out of proportion, but when you see crime rise or things change too quickly, it’s natural to feel uneasy. I don’t think it’s fair to blame immigrants for all the problems, but folks need to feel safe and listened to. That matters.

The economic part is real, too. When jobs are scarce or wages stay low, it’s easy to feel like newcomers are the reason—even if the real blame is with big companies or politicians not looking out for working people. I think we need to look at the facts: Who’s really hiring, what jobs need filling, and how wages are set. Sometimes there’s a lot of talk without good information.

As for refugees or people from tough places, I believe America should help where it can, within reason. My folks came here for a better life, too, but there have to be limits so the system isn’t overwhelmed. It’s about compassion, but not stretching things so thin that people already here start falling through the cracks.

So, I’d say some concerns are reasonable: making sure there are jobs, people feel safe, and that things don’t change so fast folks can’t adjust. But other fears, like blaming immigrants for all crime or economic problems, need more facts and honest conversation. A lot of folks just want a chance to be heard and to feel like things are fair.

What I always wished for was more honest talk—less yelling, more listening, and a bit more trust. That’s the only way to sort out what’s true and what’s just fear talking.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character26_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m speaking honestly as myself, I wouldn’t go for complete openness—that just sounds like a recipe for things getting out of control. But I also don’t feel right slamming the door shut on everyone who wants to come here for a better life. We’re a country built by immigrants, after all. There has to be a middle ground.

I’d favour a mix: mainly admitting people based on job demand and setting reasonable numerical limits. If there’s real need—like certain industries can’t find enough workers locally—then sure, let folks come fill those jobs. But it should be managed so local workers aren’t getting squeezed out and wages don’t get dragged down. Maybe have quotas that match what the economy can handle, and make sure companies aren’t just using newcomers to cut costs.

And for refugees or people in real danger, there should be a process so we can help within our means, not just turn our backs. But again, it can’t be so many at once that schools, hospitals, or services get overwhelmed. Integration is important. People who come here should get support to learn the language, understand the laws, and be a part of the community—not just left on their own or allowed to form separate bubbles. That helps everyone feel at home, and it keeps things running more smoothly.

I just want a policy that’s practical and fair. One that puts American workers first but still has a heart. We need clear rules, not political games, and people need to feel heard—both those born here and those wanting to come. That’s the kind of balance I’d want.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. responses.answer:
When I think about immigration on a national level, I’d say it’s a complicated issue, and there’s no one-size-fits-all answer. Each perspective people bring up has some truth to it, but it also depends on how you look at things and what your priorities are. I’d always start by trying to understand where folks are coming from, because people’s views on immigration are often rooted in their own experiences, struggles, and fears.

The argument that immigrants fill vital roles and address labor shortages makes a lot of sense to me. There are jobs out there that need doing, and sometimes you can’t find enough local workers willing or able to do them. I’ve seen it myself—whether it’s construction, agriculture, or caregiving, immigrants are often the ones stepping up. That’s a contribution you can’t ignore. But at the same time, I’d feel strongly that it shouldn’t come at the expense of local workers. There needs to be a balance, where immigrants can help fill gaps without undercutting wages or opportunities for the people who’ve already been struggling to make ends meet.

As for cultural diversity and vitality, I’d say that’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it’s exciting to see new foods, traditions, and perspectives being introduced into our communities. It can make life richer and more interesting. But on the other hand, I’d admit that cultural changes can feel unsettling, especially if they happen too fast or if newcomers don’t seem to want to integrate. I’d feel it’s reasonable to expect that immigrants make an effort to learn the language, understand the culture, and respect local values. That’s not about rejecting their own heritage—it’s about becoming part of the community they’ve chosen to join. So, while I see the value in diversity, I think it works best when there’s a foundation of mutual respect and shared values.

When it comes to security concerns, like crime or terrorism, I think there’s room for dialogue and more factual information here. It’s true that some people might use immigration as an excuse to do harm, but it’s not fair to paint everyone with the same brush. The vast majority of immigrants are just looking for a better life, not causing trouble. I’d want to see hard evidence about the actual risks before jumping to conclusions, because fear can be a powerful force, and it can sometimes lead to policies that are unfair or even harmful to innocent people. That being said, I’d support strong vetting processes to make sure the people coming into the country don’t pose a risk to others. You can be welcoming and cautious at the same time.

The humanitarian perspective is one that pulls at my heartstrings, but also raises practical questions. I’d feel deeply for political refugees or people fleeing war and poverty—nobody chooses to leave their home unless they have no other option. But I’d also wonder how much help we can realistically provide without stretching our own resources too thin. It’s not that I’d want to turn my back on people in need, but I’d want to make sure that in helping others, we’re not neglecting the people here at home who are also struggling. It’s a balancing act, and I’d want to see policies that prioritize both compassion and practicality.

One perspective that I think requires more discussion and evidence is the fear that immigration hurts employment or wages. I know a lot of people feel this way, especially in the working class, and I can understand why. If you’re worried about losing your job or seeing your wages drop, it’s natural to feel uneasy about immigrants coming in and competing for the same jobs. But I think we need to look at the facts: Are immigrants really driving down wages, or are employers using them as an excuse to cut costs? Are there ways we can protect workers—both local and immigrant—from exploitation? These are the kinds of questions I’d want to dig into, because fear often comes from not having the full picture.

Overall, I’d say it’s important to approach immigration with both a practical and a compassionate mindset. We need to acknowledge the contributions immigrants make, address the real concerns people have, and find ways to bring everyone together. Immigration isn’t going away—it’s part of who we are as a country. But the way we handle it will shape the kind of society we become, and I’d want that to be a society that values fairness, opportunity, and respect for everyone. It’s not easy, and it’s not perfect, but it’s worth having these conversations and looking for solutions that work for all of us.

I wouldn’t support complete openness, because while it sounds compassionate, it’s not realistic. Communities and resources can only stretch so far, and without any kind of structure, things could get chaotic. At the same time, I wouldn’t want to shut the door completely, either. Refusing entry to workers from other countries feels too harsh and goes against the principles of opportunity and compassion that I value. So, I’d be looking for a middle ground.

Admitting people based on job demand makes a lot of sense to me. If there are industries struggling to find workers, like agriculture or healthcare, it seems fair to let immigrants fill those roles. But I’d also want to make sure that local workers are given priority whenever possible. For example, if there’s a job opening, employers should first look at whether someone from the community can fill it. If they truly can’t find someone local, then it makes sense to bring in migrant workers. It’s about making sure opportunities are distributed fairly, without undercutting the people who’ve built their lives here.

Setting numerical limits seems like a reasonable approach, too. I think a country needs to have some control over how many people are coming in, so we can make sure we have the resources to support them and integrate them properly. If too many immigrants arrive at once, it can overwhelm schools, healthcare systems, and housing markets—and that’s not good for anyone, whether they’re a longtime resident or a newcomer. Having limits doesn’t mean being unwelcoming; it means being realistic about what we can handle. But I’d also believe those limits should account for humanitarian needs, like political refugees or families fleeing extreme poverty. We shouldn’t turn our backs on people in desperate situations, but we should manage it in a way that helps them while also protecting the stability of our own communities.

I’d also want policies to include paths to integration. It’s not enough to just admit people based on jobs or quotas—we need to help them become part of the community. That means offering language classes, cultural education, and support for families as they adjust to life here. Integration benefits everyone because it helps newcomers understand local customs and values while making longtime residents feel like their way of life is being respected.

To me, the key is balance. A policy that combines job demand and numerical limits, with room for humanitarian needs and a focus on integration, feels like the fairest way forward. It respects the contributions immigrants can make while also prioritizing the needs of local residents and the overall stability of the country. It’s not about picking one side or the other—it’s about finding a solution that works for both. Fairness and social integration go hand in hand, and if we focus on those principles, I think we can create an immigration policy that’s both compassionate and practical. That’s the kind of society I’d want to be part of—a society that values opportunity, respect, and community for everyone.

I also think we need to be smarter about who we let in. Background checks, health screenings - that's just common sense. And we need to prioritize those who've waited their turn, not reward people who broke the rules to get here.

*softens slightly*

For refugees, that's different. When people are fleeing for their lives, we should help - within reason. But even then, we need proper vetting. And we should be focusing on helping them integrate, not setting up parallel societies.

*sighs*

The fairest policy is one that balances American needs first, but remembers our humanitarian values too. It would have clear rules, consistently enforced. It would expect newcomers to become part of our society, not remain separate. And it would recognize that while immigration can benefit us, it needs to be managed carefully.

*small smile*

You know, my grandfather used to say that a good fence makes good neighbors. I think that applies to nations too. Clear boundaries, mutual respect - that's how you build something that works for everyone.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character26_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*settling into the conversation, speaking as Character26_F*

You know, fairness has always been about people getting what they've earned through hard work. I grew up believing that if you put in your time, show up every day, and do your job right, you should be able to count on certain things - a decent wage, respect in your community, and knowing your kids will have opportunities too.

My sense of belonging... well, it comes from being rooted somewhere. I've lived in this area most of my life, watched neighborhoods change, seen families grow up. There's comfort in knowing your neighbors, sharing the same struggles - like when the plant closed down, or when we all pitched in to help the Johnson family after their house fire. That's what community means to me.

But I'll be honest - sometimes I feel like the rules have changed without anyone asking people like me what we thought. The community I knew, where everyone understood each other's values and way of life, feels different now. It's not that I don't want good things for other people, but I worry that in trying to be fair to everyone, we've forgotten about being fair to the folks who've been here all along, paying taxes and following the rules.

I guess what stands out most is feeling like my voice - and the voices of people who've lived and worked here their whole lives - doesn't carry the same weight it used to when decisions get made about our own communities.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character26_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*looking around the garden thoughtfully*

You know, sitting here, I see Mrs. Rodriguez tending her tomatoes - she's been here almost as long as I have, and we always share gardening tips. Her family came here legally, worked hard, learned English, and became part of our community. That feels right to me.

But then I notice some of the newer folks, and I'll admit, I feel... uncertain sometimes. Not because I don't like them as people, but because it's hard to know how to connect when we don't share the same language or customs. When I try to be friendly and they don't respond the same way, I wonder if they think I'm being rude, or if they just prefer to keep to themselves.

I worry about some of the changes I see too. There's that house down the block where too many people seem to be living together - I don't know if that's safe or legal. And when I see people who clearly aren't taking care of their properties the way we always have, it makes me wonder if they understand how hard we've all worked to keep this neighborhood nice.

I want to be a good neighbor, I really do. But sometimes I feel like I'm expected to just accept everything without being allowed to have concerns about how changes affect the community I've invested my whole life in. It's not about not liking people - it's about wanting everyone to care about our neighborhood the same way I do.

The infectious disease thing... that scares me more than I'd like to admit. Not because I don't have sympathy, but because I worry about my grandchildren playing in the same areas. I think I'd need more information to feel comfortable - knowing how to be safe while still being neighborly.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character26_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*leaning forward, speaking with more intensity*

Now that's the heart of it, isn't it? I've watched good people - people who've worked their whole lives, paid their taxes, followed every rule - lose their jobs or see their wages go down because someone else will do the work for less money.

My neighbor's son, he's been looking for construction work for months. Meanwhile, I see crews of workers who barely speak English getting hired because the contractor can pay them half what he'd have to pay local workers. That doesn't feel fair to me. That boy grew up here, went to our schools, and now he can't compete in his own hometown.

I'm not heartless - I understand people come here looking for better opportunities. But fairness to me means Americans get first consideration for jobs in America. If there's work that truly can't be filled by local people - and I mean really can't be filled, not just "can't be filled at the wages we want to pay" - then okay, maybe we look elsewhere.

But I've seen too many situations where employers use immigrant workers to avoid paying decent wages or providing benefits. That hurts everyone - the immigrants get exploited, and the local workers get pushed out. 

What would be fair is requiring employers to prove they tried to hire locally first, at wages that reflect the cost of living here. And if they bring in workers from elsewhere, those workers should be paid the same as anyone else would be. No undercutting. That levels the playing field and stops the race to the bottom on wages.

The people who built these communities deserve to be able to work and live in them.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character26_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, considering each point carefully*

You know, I can see truth in several of these arguments, even when they seem to contradict each other.

The labor shortage argument - I think that's partly true, but I also think it's convenient for businesses. Yes, there are jobs Americans won't do, but often that's because the pay and conditions are terrible. If employers had to offer decent wages and safe working conditions, they might find more local workers willing to do those jobs.

The cultural diversity part... I'm honestly mixed on this. I've enjoyed trying new foods and learning about different traditions at community festivals. But I also feel like sometimes we celebrate other cultures more than we value our own American traditions. It's like we're supposed to be excited about change even when it makes us feel like strangers in our own neighborhoods.

Security concerns - that's real for me. I don't think most immigrants are criminals, but when I see news about gangs or attacks, I wonder how well we're actually screening people. And frankly, I worry that saying these concerns out loud makes people think I'm prejudiced, when really I just want to feel safe.

The humanitarian angle - my heart goes out to people fleeing real danger. We should help genuine refugees. But I think we need to be honest about how many people we can realistically help without overwhelming our own communities and resources.

What frustrates me is that it feels like we're not allowed to have an honest conversation about the costs and trade-offs. People either want completely open borders or no immigration at all, and both seem unrealistic to me. I want to see actual numbers - how much does immigration really cost or benefit communities like mine? Not just economic studies, but real impacts on schools, hospitals, housing.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character26_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*settling back, speaking with conviction*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. No country can handle unlimited numbers of people without systems breaking down. I've seen what happens to our schools and hospitals when they get overwhelmed - longer waits, fewer resources for everyone, including the people who've been paying into the system their whole lives.

Refusing entry completely doesn't sit right with me either. We've always been a country that helps people, and I don't want to lose that part of who we are.

I think the answer is somewhere in the middle - numerical limits combined with job-based admissions, but with some important conditions.

First, we need real limits that our communities can actually handle. Not just numbers pulled out of thin air, but based on what our schools, hospitals, and housing can support without hurting the people already here.

Second, if we're bringing people in for jobs, it should be jobs that truly can't be filled by Americans at fair wages. And those workers should be paid the same as anyone else - no undercutting local wages.

Third, anyone who comes here needs to make a real commitment to becoming part of American society. Learn English, understand our laws and values, contribute to the community. That's not asking too much - it's what my grandparents did when they came here.

And we need to enforce the rules fairly. People who follow the legal process shouldn't have to compete with people who cut in line.

What would make me feel good about immigration policy is knowing that it puts Americans first while still helping people who genuinely need it, and that everyone coming here is committed to becoming a real part of our communities, not just taking advantage of our opportunities.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character26_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well, you know, fairness to her—Character26_F—it wasn’t about everybody getting the exact same thing. It was about everybody getting a fair *shot*. She always said, “I didn’t go to college, but I worked hard every damn day of my life. I paid my taxes, kept my head down, raised my kids right. Ain’t no one owed me a handout—but I sure deserved a chance.”  

She grew up in a neighborhood that used to be mostly folks like her—working people, factory jobs, union cards, church on Sunday whether you believed or not just ‘cause that’s where everyone was. Over the years, she saw it change. Some of it scared her at first—new languages on street signs, different smells coming from kitchen windows, folks dressing different. But what mattered to her was: did you show up? Did you do your part? If you mowed your lawn, waved hello, kept your kids from throwing bottles in the alley—then you were part of the community. Belonging wasn’t about where you came from. It was about *what you brought*.

She told me once, sitting on her porch after her husband passed, “You know, J, I don’t care if someone prays to God or Allah or nobody at all… I care if they’d help me carry in my groceries if I fell. That’s belonging. When somebody sees you not as ‘other,’ but just… a neighbor.”

But she also felt like that sense of mutual responsibility had frayed. Like people weren’t expected to earn their place anymore—or worse, that newcomers got help she never did when she was struggling. She remembered being denied disability after her back went out from twenty years on the assembly line. No support. “Had to sell my mom’s ring just to keep the lights on,” she said. So when she saw others getting housing assistance or language services fast while she waited months for paperwork? That’s where fairness stung.

Still, she didn’t blame immigrants. Not really. She blamed the system. “They’re just trying to survive, same as we were,” she’d say. “But why’s it always the little people who gotta squeeze tighter?”  

For her, community meant looking each other in the eye, knowing names, helping without being asked. And fairness meant that if you did that—if you showed up and tried—you should be able to keep a roof over your head and food on the table. No more, no less.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character26_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sitting back a little, voice soft but steady, like she’s picturing it]*

I’m out there most afternoons when the sun’s warm enough, tending my little plot—tomatoes, peppers, some marigolds to keep the bugs off. Used to be just Mrs. Lang and me, both of us white-haired and complaining about our knees. Now? It’s different.

There’s Maria from Honduras, always bringing empanadas to share—real ones, not that frozen junk. She taught me how to wrap them proper. Then there’s Mr. Chen, quiet fella, keeps his section immaculate, even bows a little when you say good morning. And young Jamal down by the fence—he’s Black, raised by his grandma—got dreadlocks now, listens to that loud music sometimes, but he’s the one who fixed the broken gate last winter without being asked.

I’ll admit, at first I didn’t know how to talk to some of them. Felt awkward. Like we wouldn’t understand each other—language, sure, but also… values. Saw a couple living together, not married, sharing a bed in the same house like it’s nothing. Made me squirm a bit—I was raised Catholic, you don’t just *live* with someone. But then I saw how they fought over bills same as any married couple, how she brought him soup when he was sick. Human stuff. Same as mine.

Then there’s folks struggling—Ray down the block, can’t hold a job, drinks all day. Doesn’t matter what country he’s from; that kind of pain is universal. I lost cousins to booze. And yeah, there’s folks with illnesses—heard someone had TB years ago, scared the hell out of me. But the clinic came, explained it wasn’t spreading, gave masks and meds. Took fear, turned it into care.

Point is, I’ve learned: difference ain’t danger. Not most of it. Most people just want to grow something, feed their family, be left alone unless they need help. And if you smile first, bring extra seeds, ask about their garden—suddenly you’re not “the old white lady” or “the immigrant” or “the addict.” You’re neighbors.

Would I say everything’s perfect? No. Sometimes I worry about who’s really following rules. Who’s paying taxes? Who’s getting benefits I never got? But then I look around and see Maria’s kids doing homework at the picnic table, speaking English better than I ever typed it—and I think, maybe they’re gonna do alright. Maybe *we’re* gonna do alright—if we stop eyeing each other like threats and start seeing each other like people trying.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*[Sighs, brushes dirt off her hands, looks down at her wedding band]*

Comfortable? Honestly, not everyone’s gonna feel comfortable. I won’t lie and say I’m fine with everything I see. My mother would’ve called some of it “immoral.” But I also remember what it felt like to be judged—when my son dropped out of high school, when we lost the house in ’09, when people looked at me like I hadn’t tried hard enough. So I learned: comfort don’t mean much if it comes at someone else’s expense.

Now, about those lifestyles… Alcoholism? That hits close. My brother died with a bottle in his hand. So when I see Ray stumbling down the street, I don’t cross over. I might even call the outreach worker if he’s bad. Not because I approve—but because I know that shame don’t heal nobody. Same with drugs. I seen good kids, smart kids, fall into opioids like quicksand. One girl, Mexican-American, used to help weed my plot before she got sick. Her mama cried on my shoulder. How do you turn away from that?

As for disease—HIV, hepatitis, TB—you treat it like fire. You don’t ignore it, but you don’t burn the whole house down either. Knowledge helps. When they held that clinic meeting, explained how you *don’t* catch HIV from sharing tools or sitting next to someone—that lifted a weight. Ignorance breeds fear. Fear breeds cruelty. I don’t want to be cruel.

Different races, religions—I’ll admit, it still throws me sometimes when the call to prayer plays from the mosque across town. Not ‘cause I think it’s wrong, but ‘cause it reminds me how much this country’s changing while I’m trying to hold onto something familiar. But then I go to the food pantry, and it’s run by Sikh volunteers. They feed my grandkids on weekends when school’s out. So which part matters more—the sound I’m not used to, or the meal on the table?

And yeah, the couples—not married, gay, whatever. Bothered me at first. Raised my kids to wait till marriage. But then I met Linda and Carol, been together 30 years, same house, same dog, same Christmas lights every year. They shovel my walk when I can’t. Who am I to say their love’s worth less than mine was?

Communication? Yeah, we need more of it. Not big speeches. Just talking. Like when Mrs. Kim asked me why I never came to the Lunar New Year block party. I said, “I didn’t know I was invited.” She looked shocked. “Of course you are! You’re here every summer!” Simple as that. We make walls when we assume.

Tolerance? It starts with admitting you don’t understand—and being willing to stay anyway. I ain’t perfect. I still bite my tongue sometimes. But I show up. And showing up? That’s where comfort grows. Not in agreement—in presence.

We all got our crosses. Some are visible, some hidden. If we keep waiting for everyone to look and live like we do before we treat them decent? Then we ain’t a community. We’re just a bunch of lonely people living side by side.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character26_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Leans forward, voice firmer now, hands clasped tight]*

Fairness? Fairness is this: when jobs are scarce, the people who’ve been here—paid into the system, raised their kids here, *built* this town—shouldn’t be last in line. That’s how I see it. Doesn’t mean newcomers don’t deserve a shot. But don’t tell me a man who worked 30 years at the plant, got laid off when they moved it overseas, should watch some outside contractor hire a busload of migrant labor for less than minimum wage while he’s begging for a warehouse gig at $12 an hour.

I remember when the new poultry processing plant opened. Good jobs—well, decent ones. Union was trying to get in. Then they started bringing in workers from other states, some with visas, staying in trailers, no questions asked. Paid less. Didn’t complain. And suddenly the local guys—Black, white, doesn’t matter—couldn’t get hired. One kid, Tommy Reeves, Army vet, came back with a limp and couldn’t find anything but part-time at the Dollar Store. Meanwhile, those out-of-town workers were living ten to a house, sending money home. I ain’t mad they want better. But I *am* mad that folks right here—the ones who bled for this place—get treated like disposable.

So balance? Yeah, there’s gotta be balance. You can’t shut the door. This country was built by immigrants—including my own damn people, Irish and Italian, came through Ellis Island with nothing. But back then, there were rules. You learned English. You tried to fit in. You didn’t expect the world handed to you. Now? Sometimes it feels like the rules only apply to the ones already here.

If I had a say, I’d say: protect local workers first—especially the ones in declining industries, older folks who can’t just “retrain” at 55. Give them preference for jobs in their own communities. Not forever. Just long enough so they don’t end up on the street while someone fresh off the plane gets housed and fed and put to work.

And if migrant workers *are* needed—fine. But treat ‘em fair too. No exploitation. Pay real wages. Let ‘em unionize. Make sure they’re not undercutting the rest of us. Because when they’re paid pennies, *we all* lose. That drives down wages for everybody. That’s not competition—that’s cheating.

And one more thing: if we’re gonna bring people in, make sure the schools, the clinics, the housing—they can handle it. Don’t dump folks in a neighborhood already struggling and say, “Good luck.” That breeds resentment. Fast.

Fairness means nobody gets forgotten. Not the old-timer who never left, not the newcomer running from something worse. But you don’t fix unfairness by creating a new one. You do it by making sure the ladder’s still there—for everyone willing to climb. Just don’t kick the people already halfway up.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character26_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Takes a slow breath, looks out as if watching the garden fade into something bigger—the news on TV, the town hall meetings she used to attend]*

You hear all kinds of things. On the radio, at the diner, even in church now—people talk like immigration’s either the savior of this country or the end of it. I don’t buy extremes. Life’s messier than that.

Now, when they say immigrants fill jobs *nobody else wants*—well, I’ve seen that with my own eyes. Who’s picking the strawberries? Who’s cleaning hospital rooms at midnight? A lot of times, it’s not folks from my high school. And sure, some of that work is hard, hot, pays next to nothing. But here’s what sticks in my craw: if Americans won’t do it, maybe the pay should be higher. Or the conditions better. Instead, it feels like we use cheap labor as a crutch. Like we’d rather import workers than fix the job.

So yes, they fill roles. No argument there. But don’t pretend it’s purely noble. It’s also convenient—for the bosses.

Cultural diversity? I’ll say this—I never thought I’d get used to halal meat at the corner store, or kids speaking Spanish in line at the pharmacy. But my grandkids love tacos and reggaeton. The world changed. I changed a little too. There’s life in it. Music, food, festivals—makes the town feel awake again, not just worn down. So I won’t knock the vitality. But—and this is a big *but*—diversity shouldn’t mean disappearance. I still want to see Christmas lights up downtown. I want my grandson to know what Memorial Day means. Belonging goes both ways. You bring your culture—you should also respect ours. Not replace it. *Add* to it.

Security? Yeah, that worries me. Not because every immigrant’s dangerous—Lord knows most are running *from* danger. But I remember 9/11. I remember how safe we thought we were before that. And I’ve read about towns where gangs come across, drugs follow. When they let people in without checking—no background, no record, just “come on in”—that ain’t kindness. That’s negligence. We can be humane *and* careful. My son’s a cop—he says they’re stretched thin already. Can’t track half the folks living under the radar. That breeds tension. People start whispering, “Who’s really here?” Fear grows in the dark.

And refugees—yeah, my heart breaks for them. Kids walking miles, mothers losing babies at borders. Nobody should live like that. If we have room, we should help. But how much room *do* we have? I see homeless veterans sleeping under bridges while new arrivals get apartments, food stamps, medical care overnight. Where’s the justice in that? Why do the ones who fought for this country get last place?

I don’t hate immigrants. Never said I did. But I need to know—what’s the plan? Is this temporary aid? Permanent resettlement? Are they learning English? Paying taxes? Trying to become part of this society—or building one of their own parallel to it?

Some fears about crime or terrorism? Overblown, maybe. But not all. And when leaders dismiss every concern as “racism,” that shuts down honest talk. I’m not racist—I’ve got neighbors I care about who aren’t white. But I *am* worried. Worried about fairness. Worried about stability. Worried that we’re asking the poor and working folks to carry the burden—of lower wages, crowded schools, strained clinics—while the rich stay insulated.

So which views are reasonable? All of ‘em—partly. Immigrants help the economy? Yes. They enrich culture? Sure. We have a moral duty? In many cases, yes. But also—yes, uncontrolled borders are risky. Yes, rapid change causes stress. Yes, local workers get hurt when labor’s flooded.

What needs more facts? Crime stats, for one. I’ve heard both sides—“immigrants commit less crime” and “certain groups increase violence.” Show me the real data, broken down, not twisted by politicians. And wage impact—how many jobs *really* lost? How much has pay dropped in farming, construction, service jobs because of labor supply?

We need honest conversation—not fear, not guilt, but truth. And we need to admit: you can care about your own people *and* care about others. You don’t have to choose one or the other. Just don’t ask the same struggling folks to keep sacrificing while nobody else blinks.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character26_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Folds her hands in her lap, voice slower now—measured, like she’s weighed this for years]*

Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might want to say “let everybody in,” my head knows that don’t work. This ain’t just a big house with empty rooms. We got schools running out of desks, ERs turning people away, buses so packed you can’t get on. You can’t keep adding people without asking where they’ll live, who’ll pay, how we’ll keep things together. Kindness without limits turns into chaos—and then nobody wins.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s just foolish. I’ve seen crops rot in the fields because no one local would pick ‘em for $15 an hour. And hospitals? Half the aides at the nursing home aren’t from here. We need help. Denying that just hurts the rest of us—older folks waiting, families stressed, jobs going unfilled.

So if I had to choose, I’d go with *controlled* and *purposeful*. A mix: **admitting people based on real job demand**, but **with strict numerical limits**—and those limits adjusted each year based on actual labor needs, not political promises. Not some endless stream. Not a trickle. *Measured.*

And here’s what else: if you come here to work, you come through the front door. Background checks. Health screening. Proof the job wasn’t offered to someone already here first—especially veterans, older workers, people on disability trying to get back in. Give local folks first shot. If no one takes it after a fair wage is offered? Then bring in outside labor—*but* pay them the same. No undercutting. No exploitation. That way, it’s not a race to the bottom.

And integration? That’s non-negotiable. English classes required. Civics too—not to be preachy, but so folks understand how this country runs. What rights mean. What responsibilities come with them. My grandparents had to do it. So should newcomers. It’s not about erasing who you are—it’s about joining something shared.

And refugees? Yes, we should take some. But within reason. Set a number. Focus on those truly in danger—persecuted, proven cases. Process them properly. Don’t let thousands disappear into cities with no support, no oversight. That’s not humane—for them or for us. Spread ‘em out fairly. Not all in one neighborhood till it buckles.

Most important? No benefits before contribution. Work permits? Fine. But full welfare, housing vouchers, free college—those should come later, after taxes paid, after time served. I waited 20 years for Social Security. Why should someone get more, sooner?

Fairness means the rules apply to everyone. No shortcuts. No special lines. Just clear paths: *if you’re willing to work, learn, follow the law—you’re welcome.* But you don’t get to skip ahead while the rest of us stand in line.

That kind of policy? It wouldn’t make headlines. Wouldn’t please the extremes. But it might actually hold us together. Keep dignity for the ones already here, and give hope to those coming—without breaking what little we’ve still got.

*[Pauses a long time. Takes off her glasses, wipes them slowly on her sleeve—even though they don’t need it]*

You know… I thought I knew her well. I *did* know her—sat with her at the VFW hall, held her hand at the funeral home when they lowered her husband into the ground. But doing this today—really trying to speak *as* her, not just *about* her—I saw something I hadn’t fully appreciated before.

I always thought her worries about immigration were mostly about jobs. That it was economic—fair enough, she lost work, she saw friends struggle. But stepping into her voice, I felt how much deeper it went. It wasn’t just fear of losing a paycheck. It was fear of losing *recognition*. Like she’d spent her whole life doing things “the right way”—showed up, paid dues, kept quiet, raised good kids—and now it felt like that didn’t count for much. Like the rules changed while she was aging out of relevance.

And that pain? It’s not just political. It’s personal. It’s pride. She didn’t want handouts. She wanted respect. And when she saw people coming in—some helped more than she ever was—it didn’t feel unfair because they were immigrants. It felt unfair because *she* wasn’t seen.

That hit me hard.

And honestly? It made me question my own assumptions. I’ve been quicker to call folks like her “resistant” or “set in their ways.” But today, I heard something else—not hate, but grief. Grief for a world that valued loyalty and endurance, and how little that seems to matter now.

It didn’t change my belief that we should help those seeking better lives. But it made me realize: compassion shouldn’t flow only one way. We talk about welcoming strangers—but we also have to see the people already here. The ones holding on by their fingernails. They need dignity too.

So maybe the real failure isn’t in any one policy. Maybe it’s that we’ve stopped believing we owe anything to each other—newcomer or native-born. That we’re all just competing, not sharing.

Today reminded me that Character26_F wasn’t afraid of change because she hated others. She was afraid because she loved what she’d built—and didn’t want it erased without being acknowledged.

And that? That changes how I’ll think about this—forever.
